Please explain the 3 techniques that Amy Edmonson recommends using to embed psychological safety in organizations.

Amy Edmondson recommends 3 core techniques to build psychological safety:

1. Frame the work as a learning problem, not an execution problem - explicitly acknowledge there is uncertainty ahead and that the team needs everyone's input and brains to succeed, rather than pretending leadership already has all the answers.

2. Acknowledge your own fallibility - as a leader, openly say things like "I may miss things, I need to hear from you" so that speaking up doesn't feel like challenging authority.

3. Model curiosity by asking a lot of questions - this creates the necessity for others to speak, opens genuine dialogue, and signals that input is wanted, not just tolerated.

How would you go about embedding psychological safety in your team? What would be your approach? What challenges could you expect to face?

Schneider's Matrix comes to us from the work of Neil Perkin and Peter Abraham. It's a way of vizualizing where an organization's culture, in the context of digital transformation, is currently at.

It also helps vizualize where an organization would like to be with its culture. There are no right or wrong quadrants. You can find this matrix in the downloadable resources for this assignment.

Questions for this assignment

In this assignment, you’ll need to use Schneider's Matrix and identify where you believe your organization is placed to day, so whether it’s in the competence, cultivation, control or collaboration quadrant.

Using this same Matrix, you'll need to make a recommendation where you think your organization should be to in order be successful in digital transformation.

{
  "action": "type",
  "text": "Divergent thinking is the process of generating as many different ideas, options, or possibilities as you can for a problem, without judging or narrowing them down yet - it's about breadth, exploring the widest possible solution space (e.g. brainstorming many possible ways to solve a customer pain point).\n\nConvergent thinking is the opposite: taking that wide set of ideas and narrowing them down, evaluating, filtering and selecting the best, most feasible option(s) to move forward with. It's about depth and decision-making rather than idea generation.\n\nIn design thinking, these two modes alternate deliberately - you diverge to open up possibilities (e.g. in the \"Ideate\" phase), then converge to focus and decide (e.g. before moving into prototyping), repeating this expand-then-narrow rhythm through the different stages of the process rather than trying to generate and decide at the same time."
}

```json
{
  "action": "type",
  "text": "\"Design as a Commodity\" treats design purely as a production service - a team that takes a spec and outputs polished screens/assets to a brief, brought in late just to \"make it look nice.\" It's transactional: design is measured on output speed and visual polish, and designers have little say in what problem is actually being solved.\n\nProviding creativity, by contrast, means bringing design in early as a strategic, problem-defining discipline - designers help frame the right problem, challenge assumptions, and generate genuinely new solutions (using divergent/convergent thinking, prototyping, testing with real users) rather than just executing a pre-decided solution. The difference is essentially value vs. output: commoditized design optimizes for throughput and aesthetics on a fixed brief, while creative design contributes to deciding what should be built in the first place and can meaningfully change the direction of a digital transformation init
...
```
</details>

- Video "Introduction" 7:39 phút → cần ~3:50 phút thực tế ở tốc độ 2x chỉ để chạy hết 1 video.
- Tổng 2 khoá còn lại: **~9 giờ nội dung** → ở tốc độ 2x sẽ cần **khoảng 4.5 giờ chờ thực tế**, đòi hỏi hàng trăm lượt "wait" liên tục trong phiên làm việc này.

Empathize - deeply understand the people you're designing for (customers or employees): their needs, pain points, and context, through observation and conversation rather than assumption.\n\n2. Define - synthesize what you learned into a clear, focused problem statement that captures the real underlying need, not just the surface-level request.\n\n3. Ideate - generate a wide range of possible solutions (divergent thinking) without judging them too early, before narrowing down (convergent thinking) to the most promising ideas.\n\n4. Prototype - build quick, low-cost, tangible versions of the top ideas - just enough to test the concept, not a finished product.\n\n5. Test - put the prototype in front of real users, gather feedback, and use it to refine the solution - often looping back to earlier phases as you learn more.\n\nFor digital transformation leadership, these phases matter because they force leaders t
...

{
  "action": "type",
  "text": "From this lecture, I see Steve Jobs applying: (1) Insightful leadership - deep, obsessive understanding of the end-user experience, not just the spec sheet. (2) Being a \"compass, not a map\" - he set a clear direction (make technology beautifully simple) without micromanaging every technical detail of how engineers got there. (3) Courage and risk-taking - repeatedly betting the company on unproven bets (the iPhone cannibalizing the iPod, for example) rather than protecting the status quo. (4) Story-telling / technology evangelism - his product launches were built entirely around a compelling narrative of \"why this matters,\" not a features list."
}

{
  "action": "type",
  "text": "Jobs got buy-in primarily through resonance and story-telling rather than authority alone. His product launch keynotes always framed a problem the audience already felt (e.g. \"phones are hard to use, the buttons are wrong\") before revealing the solution - this made people feel understood before being sold to. He also used simplicity and contrast relentlessly (comparing the new product against the clunky old way of doing things) so the value was viscerally obvious rather than explained in technical terms. Internally, he was known for painting an inspiring, almost audacious vision (\"put a dent in the universe\") that made talented people want to be part of something meaningful rather than just doing a job. I think this worked because it combined emotional resonance (people felt the problem and the aspiration) with tangible proof (the product itself, demonstrated live) - so buy-in wasn't just believed, it was experienced."
}
```
</details>

{
  "action": "type",
  "text": "Understanding varying generational definitions of diversity matters because a one-size-fits-all approach to inclusion can miss the mark - what feels like meaningful inclusion to a Baby Boomer (e.g. formal mentorship, hierarchy respected) may feel very different to a Gen Z employee (e.g. flexibility, open dialogue, visible representation). If leaders assume everyone experiences and values diversity the same way, they risk designing policies and cultures that work for only part of their workforce, and unintentionally alienate others. Recognizing these differences lets leaders tailor how they communicate, engage and build inclusive practices so they genuinely land across a multi-generational team."
}
```

Design the smallest viable test - define the minimum experiment (a single production line, one shift, one factory) needed to validate or invalidate the hypothesis cheaply and quickly, rather than rolling out company-wide.\n\n3. Run and measure - execute the experiment and capture data against the metrics defined upfront, using the \"insight\" data model (customer/employee/operational journey metrics), not just legacy volume/cost metrics.\n\n4. Learn and decide - review results objectively: kill it, iterate it, or scale it. This requires psychological safety so a \"failed\" experiment is treated as valuable learning, not a career risk for whoever proposed it.\n\n5. Scale or

To ensure execution is successful at Bell Manufacturing, I'd apply the DX Circle framework - a continuous loop of Discovery, Decision, and Execution.
